demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Margaret's Burden

Margaret has worked security at the Westfield shopping center for nearly twenty years. She knows the layout of the building better than she knows her own home—every entrance, every camera angle, every blind spot. At sixty-one, she's the most senior guard on the day shift, the one newer staff members ask for advice. She takes pride in that. The job has given her structure and purpose after her divorce, a reason to get up each morning in a uniform that means something.

The incident happened on a Tuesday in March, on what seemed like an ordinary afternoon. Margaret was escorting a shoplifter—a young man, maybe twenty-five—toward the security office. He'd been caught on camera taking merchandise. She'd done this hundreds of times before: professional, firm, but not unkind. As they approached the stairs, the man suddenly turned and tried to run. Margaret reached out to stop him, her hand catching his arm. In the struggle, he lost his footing. She can still see it—the way his body seemed to fold as he fell down the concrete stairwell. The sound his head made when it hit the landing.

He survived, but barely. A fractured skull, bleeding in the brain, weeks in intensive care. Margaret learned later that he had a daughter. The investigation cleared her of wrongdoing—the footage showed he'd initiated contact, that she'd acted within protocol. But the investigation couldn't change what happened.

Since that day in March, Margaret hasn't slept properly. She lies awake at night replaying those seconds, her mind insisting there was something else she could have done, some different way she could have moved. Around 3 a.m., she usually gives up on sleep and sits on her couch with the television on, though she rarely watches it. Sometimes she imagines the man's daughter—a girl she's never seen—looking at her with accusation. That image appears without warning, sometimes multiple times an hour.

Going to work has become an ordeal. The stairwell where it happened now feels dangerous in a way she can't quite explain. She finds herself avoiding it, taking the longer route through the loading area. Her hands shake when she has to approach someone who's behaving aggressively or erratically. Last month, a teenager ran from a store, and Margaret felt her chest tighten so severely she thought she was having a heart attack. She sat in the break room for an hour, unable to move.

She's called in sick more times in the past eight months than in the previous five years combined. Her supervisor has noticed. There's talk of her taking medical leave, maybe early retirement. The thought terrifies her—without this job, who is she? But the thought of going back also terrifies her.

At home, Margaret isolates. She used to go to the RSA club on Friday nights with coworkers, but she hasn't been in months. She declined her sister's invitation to her grandson's birthday party. Even watching the news makes her anxious; any story about an accident or injury sends her spiraling. She's aware that she's become difficult to be around, that she snaps at people over small things. She feels the weight of what she's done pressing down constantly, even though intellectually she knows the investigation cleared her.

Margaret sits in the chair across from me and says she doesn't know why she's here. She says she just needs to move on. But her eyes are hollow, and her hands won't stop moving in her lap. She tells me she's thinking about requesting the early retirement, about letting go of the only identity she's had for two decades. She says this quietly, as if admitting defeat.
